{{Short description|Statistical Model}}
{{technical|date=March 2019}}
A '''hidden semi-Markov model''' (HSMM) is a [[statistical model]] with the same structure as a [[hidden Markov model]] except that the unobservable process is [[semi-Markov process|semi-Markov]] rather than [[Markov process|Markov]]. This means that the probability of there being a change in the hidden state depends on the amount of time that has elapsed since entry into the current state. This is in contrast to hidden Markov models where there is a constant probability of changing state given survival in the state up to that time.<ref>{{citation|first=Shun-Zheng|last=Yu|title=Hidden Semi-Markov Models|journal=Artificial Intelligence|volume=174|issue=2|pages=215–243|doi=10.1016/j.artint.2009.11.011|year=2010|s2cid=1899849 }}.</ref>

For instance {{harvtxt|Sansom|Thomson|2001}} modelled daily rainfall using a hidden semi-Markov model.<ref>{{citation|first1=J.|last1=Sansom|first2=P. J.|last2=Thomson|title=Fitting hidden semi-Markov models to breakpoint rainfall data|journal=J. Appl. Probab.|volume=38A|year=2001|pages=142–157|doi=10.1239/jap/1085496598|s2cid=123113970 }}.</ref> If the underlying process (e.g. weather system) does not have a [[geometric distribution|geometrically distributed]] duration, an HSMM may be more appropriate.

Hidden semi-Markov models can be used in implementations of statistical parametric [[speech synthesis]] to model the probabilities of transitions between different states of encoded speech representations. They are often used along with other tools such [[Artificial_neural_network|artificial neural networks]], connecting with other components of a full parametric speech synthesis system to generate the output waveforms.<ref>{{citation|first1=Keiichi|last1=Tokuda|first2=Kei|last2=Hashimoto|first3=Keiichiro|last3=Oura|first4=Yoshihiko|last4=Nankaku|title=Temporal modeling in neural network based statistical parametric speech synthesis|journal=9th ISCA Speech Synthesis Workshop|volume=9|year=2016|pages=1|url=http://ssw9.talp.cat/papers/ssw9_OS2-2_Tokuda.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210313022513/http://ssw9.talp.cat/papers/ssw9_OS2-2_Tokuda.pdf|archive-date=2021-03-13}}</ref>

The model was first published by [[Leonard E. Baum]] and Ted Petrie in 1966.<ref>{{Cite book | last1 = Barbu | first1 = V. | last2 = Limnios | first2 = N. | chapter = Hidden Semi-Markov Model and Estimation | doi = 10.1007/978-0-387-73173-5_6 | title = Semi-Markov Chains and Hidden Semi-Markov Models toward Applications | series = Lecture Notes in Statistics | volume = 191 | pages = 1 | year = 2008 | isbn = 978-0-387-73171-1 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Baum | first1 = L. E. | author-link1 = Leonard E. Baum| last2 = Petrie | first2 = T. | doi = 10.1214/aoms/1177699147 | title = Statistical Inference for Probabilistic Functions of Finite State Markov Chains | journal = The Annals of Mathematical Statistics | volume = 37 | issue = 6 | pages = 1554 | year = 1966 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

[[Statistical inference]] for hidden semi-Markov models is more difficult than in hidden Markov models, since algorithms like the [[Baum–Welch algorithm]] are not directly applicable, and must be adapted requiring more resources.
